accepted: A region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron. Each orbital can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins.

content.text: Think about where the electron is likely to be, then the capacity and spins of one orbital.

workedAnswer.text: A region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron. Each orbital can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins.
An orbital is a region around the nucleus.
It has a high probability of containing an electron.
One orbital holds a maximum of two electrons.
Paired electrons have opposite spins.

An orbital is a region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron. It can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins; it is not a fixed path around the nucleus.

context.text: What is the name given to a region of space around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron.

content.text: The term has two words; the second begins with o.

workedAnswer.text: atomic orbital
Atomic orbital.
An atomic orbital describes the region where an electron is likely to be found, rather than an orbit or fixed electron path.

context.text: What is the name given to a group of orbitals of the same type within an electron shell, such as s, p, d or f orbitals.

content.text: A shell is divided into these groups.

workedAnswer.text: Accepted alternatives: sub-shell; electron sub-shell
Subshell (electron subshell).
A subshell groups orbitals of the same type within a shell. For example, the 2p subshell contains three p orbitals.

context.text: What is the name given to a group of orbitals with the same principal quantum number, broadly associated with a particular energy and distance from the nucleus.

content.text: The principal quantum number identifies this larger grouping.

workedAnswer.text: Accepted alternatives: shell; electron shell
Electron shell (principal energy level).
Orbitals with the same principal quantum number belong to one electron shell. For example, 2s and 2p orbitals belong to the second shell.

accepted: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

content.text: Consider the force between particles with different signs of charge.

workedAnswer.text: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Electrostatic attraction.
Between oppositely charged ions.
Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions. Electron transfer forms ions; the bond itself is the attraction between them.

context.text: How many s orbitals exist in each electron shell?

content.text: Count orbitals, not the number of electrons they can hold.

workedAnswer.text: One s orbital.
Each s subshell contains one orbital, so it can hold up to two electrons.

context.text: How many p orbitals exist in each electron shell?

content.text: A p subshell can hold six electrons, with up to two in each orbital.

workedAnswer.text: Three p orbitals.
A p subshell contains three orbitals and holds up to six electrons. A p subshell exists from the second shell onwards; the first shell has only an s subshell.

context.text: How many d orbitals exist in each electron shell?

content.text: A d subshell can hold ten electrons, with up to two in each orbital.

workedAnswer.text: Five d orbitals.
A d subshell contains five orbitals and holds up to ten electrons. A d subshell exists from the third shell onwards.

context.text: What type of structure do all ionic compounds have?

content.text: Name both the type of bonding and the extended structure.

workedAnswer.text: Giant ionic lattice
A giant ionic lattice.
The source answer applies to solid ionic compounds. The ordered lattice is disrupted on melting or dissolving.

accepted: The electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and 2 positive nuclei.

content.text: Identify the negative particles being shared and the positive centres that attract them.

workedAnswer.text: The electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and 2 positive nuclei.
Strong electrostatic attraction.
Involving a shared pair of electrons.
Between that pair and the nuclei of both bonded atoms.
A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms.

accepted: Repeating pattern in the physical and chemical properties of elements when arranged in order of increasing atomic number

content.text: Think of recurring properties and the number that orders the modern periodic table.

workedAnswer.text: Repeating pattern in the physical and chemical properties of elements when arranged in order of increasing atomic number
A repeating pattern in physical and chemical properties.
Elements arranged by increasing atomic number.
Periodicity describes the repeating pattern in properties as atomic number increases. This linked recall card comes from the supplied set and connects electron structure to the Periodicity topic.

context.text: Define the term: giant ionic lattice

accepted: A repeating pattern of oppositely charged ions

content.text: Give the arrangement and name the charged particles.

workedAnswer.text: A repeating pattern of oppositely charged ions
A repeating or regular pattern.
Of oppositely charged ions.
A giant ionic lattice is a repeating, three-dimensional arrangement of positive and negative ions. The particles are ions, not neutral atoms or molecules.

context.text: Define the term: dative / coordinate bond?

accepted: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are donated by the same atom.

content.text: The distinguishing feature is where the shared pair came from.

workedAnswer.text: A covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
Both electrons in the shared pair are donated.
The same atom supplies both electrons.
In a dative covalent or coordinate bond, one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair. Once formed, it is a covalent bond.

context.text: Define the term: average bond enthalpy.

accepted: the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over a range of different compounds.

content.text: Include what happens to the bonds, the amount, the physical state and what is averaged.

workedAnswer.text: the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over a range of different compounds.
Energy required to break the specified covalent bond.
One mole of those bonds.
Bonds in gaseous molecules.
Averaged over a range of different compounds.

Average bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous molecules, averaged over different compounds. It measures covalent bond strength and links to the Enthalpy topic.
